A.label: Strong
A.meaning: Repeatedly tested in people, with results that agree.

B.label: Good
B.meaning: Solid human studies, with some room left for argument.

C.label: Mixed
C.meaning: Reasonable evidence, smaller studies, or results that conflict.

D.label: Thin
D.meaning: Early or indirect evidence. Worth trying, not worth promising.

E.label: Practice
E.meaning: No trial behind it. Widely used, and openly labelled as experience rather than proof.

practices.title: Morning light
practices.summary: Ten minutes of outdoor light within an hour of waking.
practices.why: Bright morning light sets the body clock that decides when you get sleepy — the single cheapest lever for falling asleep easier at night and feeling alert earlier in the day.
practices.safety: Never look at the sun directly; through-window light counts for less but still counts.

practices.title: Wind-down breathing
practices.summary: A short screens-away wind-down with slow breathing before bed.
practices.why: Long, slow exhales shift the nervous system toward rest; a consistent pre-sleep routine is one of the most reliable sleep-quality improvements there is.
practices.safety: A steadying tool, not treatment for a sleep disorder.

practices.title: Strength training
practices.summary: Resistance training most days you can manage — compound lifts first.
practices.why: Muscle mass and strength are among the strongest known predictors of healthy later life; strength work is the closest thing to a retirement account for the body.
practices.safety: Conservative loading, full range you control. No pushing through joint pain.

practices.title: Easy cardio, talking pace
practices.summary: Steady "can still hold a conversation" cardio — brisk walk, easy ride, easy jog. Coaches call it Zone 2.
practices.why: Easy aerobic volume builds the mitochondrial base tied to metabolic health and endurance — the biggest return per unmiserable minute for most people.
practices.safety: If you can only gasp out words, ease off — conversational pace is the point.

practices.title: Hard intervals
practices.summary: Once a week: four rounds of ~4 minutes hard, ~4 minutes easy. The kind that lifts your peak aerobic fitness (VO₂ max).
practices.why: Peak aerobic capacity correlates with long-term health more strongly than almost any other fitness measure, and one weekly interval session moves it.
practices.safety: Build up over weeks; skip when unwell; hard means hard for you, not a number.

practices.title: The daily walk
practices.summary: A brisk 30–40 minute walk, most days — the most underrated training there is.
practices.why: Walking is easy cardio in disguise: it builds the same steady fitness, costs no willpower, and is the physical activity people actually sustain for decades.
practices.safety: Brisk means you can talk but you notice the pace. Weather is not a reason; clothing is a solution.

practices.title: Post-meal walk
practices.summary: A ten-to-fifteen-minute walk after the day’s biggest meal.
practices.why: Light movement after eating blunts the glucose spike a meal produces — a tiny habit with an outsized metabolic effect.

practices.title: Ten-minute mobility
practices.summary: Ten minutes of hips, ankles and shoulders, twice a week.
practices.why: Stability and range are what let every other kind of training continue into later decades — the piece that decides whether you can still get off the floor at 80.
practices.safety: Range you control, never bounced into. Discomfort fine, pain no.

practices.title: Cold-shower finish
practices.summary: End the morning shower with 30–60 seconds cold.
practices.why: Brief deliberate cold reliably spikes alertness and mood chemistry for hours — and practising the first uncomfortable minute is rehearsal for every urge you’ll surf later.
practices.safety: Uncomfortable, never painful. Heart conditions → clinician first. Never combine cold water with open water alone.

practices.title: Protein-first breakfast
practices.summary: Roughly 30 g of protein within a couple of hours of waking.
practices.why: A protein-anchored first meal steadies appetite and energy for the whole day and front-loads the daily protein target where it’s easiest to hit.

practices.title: Caffeine cutoff
practices.summary: Last caffeine of the day, ten hours before your bedtime.
practices.why: Caffeine’s half-life is 5–6 hours: a quarter of that afternoon coffee is still circulating at midnight, quietly shaving deep sleep you never see. Ten hours leaves only a trace by lights-out.

practices.title: Weekly meal sketch
practices.summary: Fifteen Sunday minutes deciding the week’s dinners — protein first, mostly whole foods.
practices.why: Deciding once removes seven days of willpower decisions. Anchoring each meal on protein (~1.6–2.2 g/kg/day across the day) protects muscle and keeps you full.

practices.title: Kitchen closes
practices.summary: A consistent last bite by three hours before bed; eat within a daylight window.
practices.why: A steady, earlier eating window supports sleep and metabolic rhythm; late eating works against both.
practices.safety: Structure, not restriction — skip this protocol entirely if eating windows are a fraught topic for you.

practices.title: Hold the eating window
practices.summary: A consistent daily eating window — first bite and last bite at roughly the same times.
practices.why: Consistency beats duration: a steady window supports metabolic rhythm and quietly caps grazing, without counting anything.
practices.safety: Not for everyone — skip entirely if pregnant, underweight, or if restriction has ever been a fraught topic. Protein and training quality come first.

practices.title: If-then the week’s food
practices.summary: Turn each dinner into “on Tuesday, after work, I cook X” — then write the shopping list that makes it possible.
practices.why: Naming the exact when, where and first move is among the best-replicated findings in behaviour-change research, and it has been tested on food specifically rather than borrowed from elsewhere: planning the meal beats intending to eat better. The written list is the same mechanism moved to the shop — you arrive keeping a decision you already made, instead of making it hungry in an aisle built to change your mind.

practices.title: Set the default, not the willpower
practices.summary: Serve at the stove, put the packet away before you sit down, and keep the smaller bowl the one within reach.
practices.why: What is put in front of people changes how much they eat: bigger portions and bigger packages reliably lead to more eaten, pooled across dozens of randomised experiments. One honest caveat we would rather state than hide — several famous plate-size demonstrations came from a lab whose work was later retracted, so this protocol claims the portion and package finding, which stands without them, and not the plate.
practices.safety: Structure, not restriction — nothing here is counted and there is no target. Skip it entirely if how much you eat is a fraught topic for you.

practices.title: Cook at home most nights
practices.summary: Hold a set number of home-cooked dinners a week — three is a real change for most people.
practices.why: Across large national surveys in several countries, people who cook at home more often eat more vegetables and fibre and less added sugar and salt. Consistent, but observational: home cooking travels with time, money and a dozen other habits, so how much of it is the cooking itself is genuinely unknown.

practices.title: Decide before you arrive
practices.summary: Eating out this week? Choose your order from the menu online, hours before you sit down.
practices.why: Choosing in advance and choosing at the table are two different decisions made by two different versions of you — the second one is hungry, in company, and already holding bread. Field experiments on ordering ahead find the earlier choice is usually the one people would stand behind later, though the studies are few and mostly ran in canteens rather than restaurants.

practices.title: Cook once, eat twice
practices.summary: Pick one dish a week that doubles — cook the big pan on Sunday and Wednesday already has a dinner.
practices.why: The mechanism is friction rather than nutrition: a cooked meal in the fridge wins the night you are flattest, when the real competition is a delivery app. Widely taught by people who cook for a living, and it follows from what we know about defaults and effort — but we found no trial testing batch cooking itself, so it is graded low on purpose.
practices.safety: Food safety, not diet: cool leftovers fast, into the fridge inside two hours, eat within a couple of days, and reheat once until properly steaming.

practices.title: Sauna sessions
practices.summary: Two to four sauna sessions a week, ~15–20 minutes at a heat you tolerate well.
practices.why: Regular sauna use is associated in long-running Finnish cohort studies with lower cardiovascular risk, and reliably helps relaxation and sleep.
practices.safety: Hydrate; no alcohol around sessions; heart conditions or pregnancy → talk to a clinician first.

practices.title: Ten minutes of stillness
practices.summary: A short daily sit — breath as the anchor, thoughts allowed to pass.
practices.why: The single most common daily practice among the high performers Ferriss has interviewed; short consistent sessions measurably improve attention and stress recovery.
practices.safety: Non-clinical; no therapeutic claims.

practices.title: Afternoon deep rest
practices.summary: Ten to twenty minutes lying still and awake in the afternoon dip — not a nap, and not asleep.
practices.why: A guided deep-rest protocol restores alertness and lowers stress without a nap’s grogginess — a legal performance enhancer for the second half of the day.

practices.title: Five-minute journal
practices.summary: Five written minutes: what went well, what you’re grateful for, one line for tomorrow.
practices.why: Brief written gratitude and reflection reliably improve mood and sleep quality, and writing forces the clarity that vague rumination never reaches.

practices.title: Creative block
practices.summary: Two protected sessions a week for the creative thing — making, not consuming.
practices.why: Creative practice is the most common thread among people who describe their weeks as good ones — and it only happens when it has a defended place on the calendar.

practices.title: Weekly money check-in
practices.summary: Thirty Sunday minutes: automate the transfer first, then review the week’s money.
practices.why: Automation beats willpower budgeting — pay the goal first and the review becomes observation, not judgement. A weekly cadence catches drift while it’s still small.

practices.title: Fear-setting
practices.summary: Define the decision you’re avoiding: worst case, how you’d prevent it, how you’d repair it.
practices.why: Stalled decisions are usually unexamined fears. Writing the worst case down shrinks it to actual size — the exercise Ferriss credits for his biggest moves. Monthly is plenty.

practices.title: Deep work block
practices.summary: A protected 60–90 minute single-task block before the day fragments.
practices.why: The highest-leverage work is the kind interruptions kill. One protected morning block routinely outproduces a scattered afternoon.

practices.title: Weekly business review
practices.summary: A weekly structured review: what moved, what stalled, the one lever for next week.
practices.why: Aim, articulate, adjust: writing down what you’re actually aiming at — and confronting what happened — is the core discipline both Peterson and Ferriss teach for any serious goal.

practices.title: 80/20 audit
practices.summary: Roughly monthly: name the 20% producing most of the results — and the 20% producing most of the drag.
practices.why: A small share of activities produces most of the outcome; naming and cutting the drag is where leverage actually comes from.

practices.title: Sunday week preview
practices.summary: Fifteen Sunday-evening minutes looking at the week ahead: the three things that matter, the one conflict to defuse now.
practices.why: The Sunday reset — meals decided, money checked, week previewed — is the ritual stack that makes Monday start already-won instead of already-behind.

practices.title: Reach out, make a plan
practices.summary: One message a week that turns into a concrete plan with someone you like.
practices.why: Strong relationships are the most consistent predictor of long-term wellbeing in the research — and they run on logistics, not sentiment.

practices.title: The first five minutes
practices.summary: The first five minutes back together get your attention before anything else does.
practices.why: Work stress reliably follows people home as withdrawal; daily-diary research finds the reunion sets the tone for the whole evening, which makes five deliberate minutes the cheapest place to spend attention.

practices.title: Name one thing
practices.summary: Say one specific thing you noticed and valued about them — out loud, most days.
practices.why: Happy couples run a lopsided ratio of warm to sour moments. Diary studies and small experiments link specific, spoken appreciation to feeling valued — and to raising hard things more easily.

practices.title: Weekly two-of-you check-in
practices.summary: Twenty minutes on Sunday: the week ahead, who carries what, one thing each of you needs.
practices.why: How fairly the load feels shared tracks closely with satisfaction in survey after survey. The meeting itself is untested — a heuristic for making the invisible load visible before it becomes an argument.
practices.safety: A logistics conversation, not a grievance hearing. If the same subject keeps ending badly, that is a sign to talk to a couples therapist — not to hold more meetings.

practices.title: State of us
practices.summary: Roughly monthly, forty-five unhurried minutes on the relationship itself, not the logistics.
practices.why: The few randomised trials here found brief structured reflection — minutes a year, not hours a week — slowed the ordinary decline in satisfaction about as well as full skills courses did.
practices.safety: Educational structure, not couples therapy. If this conversation reliably turns into the same fight, or either of you dreads it, a couples therapist is the right next step.

practices.title: Repair, rehearsed
practices.summary: Ten written minutes on the last friction: what set it off, and the words that would have cooled it.
practices.why: Stable couples are not the ones who avoid conflict, they are the ones who de-escalate early. The repair itself happens in the moment; what you can practise beforehand is the phrase you reach for.
practices.safety: Private reflection on your own part, never a case file on your partner. Out of scope entirely where there is fear, coercion or anything you would call abuse — that needs a professional, and support lines exist for exactly this.

practices.title: The booked-in family adventure
practices.summary: One family outing a week, chosen and in the calendar before the week starts.
practices.why: Experiences tend to buy more lasting happiness than possessions, and the calendar entry is what turns the intention into an actual Saturday. Effect sizes are modest and debated.
practices.safety: Match the outing to the youngest child’s stamina — an adventure nobody enjoyed is worse than a slow morning at home.

practices.title: One-on-one with each child
practices.summary: Twenty-odd minutes a week with each child, one at a time, doing what they choose.
practices.why: Child-led one-to-one time is a building block of parenting programmes that have been trialled properly, though it has rarely been tested on its own.
practices.safety: Let the child pick and lead. If it starts feeling like an appointment they have to perform at, make it shorter or let it go.

practices.title: Stretch the anticipation
practices.summary: Fifteen minutes a week on the next trip: one decision made, one detail shared with everyone going.
practices.why: Holidaymakers report more happiness before a trip than after it, so booking early may be where much of the benefit lives — an observational finding we extend on purpose.
practices.safety: Keep plans loose enough to change. Building a trip up as the thing that will fix a hard year sets everyone up to be let down.

practices.title: The device-free family meal
practices.summary: A shared evening meal on set nights, with every phone out of the room.
practices.why: Frequent shared meals are associated with better diet and psychosocial outcomes in children across many studies — all observational, and such families differ in other ways too.
practices.safety: Aim only at the nights that are realistic. Conversation, not inspection — a meal that becomes a performance review stops being the good thing here.

practices.title: Look back at it together
practices.summary: Ten Sunday minutes going through the week’s photos, out loud, together.
practices.why: Savouring a good moment on purpose has small experimental support for lifting mood, and it stretches an experience past the day it happened. The studies are small and short.
practices.safety: Follow what the child wants to talk about, and skip anything anyone found upsetting. Educational structure, never a wellbeing intervention.

practices.title: One unmoveable family ritual
practices.summary: One small thing that happens at the same time every week, whoever else is busy.
practices.why: Predictable family routines are associated with steadier child wellbeing across decades of research — most of it correlational, so the arrow’s direction is unsettled.
practices.safety: Small and repeatable beats big and abandoned. If it turns into an obligation everyone dreads, change the ritual rather than defend it.

practices.title: Payday transfer, set once
practices.summary: Set the payday transfer so the saving leaves automatically, before any of it can be spent.
practices.why: Large workplace field trials found that making saving the default moves how much people keep far more than intention or budgeting does. The transfer is the intervention — you decide once.
practices.safety: Where the money lands — account type, product, tax treatment — is a licensed adviser or accountant question. IntentNorth helps you build the habit of the transfer, nothing more. Education, never financial advice.

practices.title: Spend the raise before it arrives
practices.summary: Once a quarter, write down what share of the next pay rise or bonus goes straight to the transfer.
practices.why: Committing income you do not hold yet avoids the sting of giving up money you do — the mechanism behind the best-known escalating-saving programme. A pay rise is when lifestyle quietly expands.
practices.safety: Choosing a share is a habit, not an allocation plan — pension, tax and investment choices belong with a licensed adviser. Education, never financial advice.

practices.title: Recurring-charge audit
practices.summary: Once a quarter, list every recurring charge and cancel what you would not sign up for again today.
practices.why: Card and billing data show recurring payments run on for years on inattention alone — people cancel when something finally forces them to look. The audit is that forcing function.
practices.safety: Check what a cancellation actually ends before you cancel it — insurance, indemnity and health cover can be far harder to restart than to stop.

practices.title: Pick a debt order you will finish
practices.summary: Monthly: list every balance with its rate, choose one order, and automate the extra payment against the first one only.
practices.why: Highest rate first costs least on paper; the follow-through evidence is mixed and leans to smallest balance first, since closing an account is visible progress. Finishing matters more than the order.
practices.safety: If payments are already being missed, or a lender is chasing, that is a licensed debt adviser or a nonprofit debt charity — not a habit app. Education, never financial advice.

practices.title: Sleep on it, then decide
practices.summary: Optional spending over a threshold you set waits 72 hours on a list; twice a week, buy only what still earns it.
practices.why: Wanting is loudest in the moment and fades on its own, so the delay hands the call to the calm version of you. Present bias is well evidenced; the rule itself is a heuristic to test on yourself.
practices.safety: The delay is for optional spending only — never postpone medical care, repairs that worsen, or anything with a real deadline.

practices.title: Quarterly position check
practices.summary: Once a quarter, write everything owned minus everything owed as one number, in the same place each time.
practices.why: Meta-analytic work on goal pursuit finds that monitoring progress, and writing it down, makes reaching a goal more likely; the effect is general, not money-specific. Quarterly catches drift without chasing noise.
practices.safety: A position number is a measurement, not a verdict on what to do next — investment, pension and tax decisions belong with a licensed professional. Education, never financial advice.

practices.title: If-then plan the week
practices.summary: Ten Monday minutes turning each commitment into “if X, then Y” — including the line that defends the deep block.
practices.why: Naming the exact when, where and first move — plus one coping line for the obstacle you can already see — is among the best-replicated findings in behaviour-change research: medium-sized effects across roughly a hundred studies, largest for intentions that keep slipping.

practices.title: Decision journal
practices.summary: Twenty Friday minutes: log each consequential call — expectation, confidence, review date — and reread what’s due.
practices.why: Knowing how it turned out overwrites what you actually believed, so experience alone teaches badly. A written forecast with a confidence number and a booked reread restores the feedback loop that calibration research shows sharpens judgement.
practices.safety: Your own calls, not a file on other people — a journal that might be read as a performance record stops being honest.

practices.title: Pre-mortem before the one-way door
practices.summary: Before a commitment that is hard to undo: assume a year has passed and it failed, then write every reason why.
practices.why: Treating the failure as already certain gets people to generate more concrete reasons than asking what might go wrong — one classic experiment, consistent with wider “consider the opposite” work. Whether it improves real outcomes is untested.
practices.safety: A thinking tool, not a veto. Run it on the calls that are hard to undo and let reversible ones stay fast.

practices.title: One-on-one cadence
practices.summary: A standing weekly half-hour per direct — their agenda, one blocker question, feedback about the work not the person.
practices.why: Manager-relationship quality tracks with engagement and retention, but that evidence is mostly observational. The firmer part is narrower: in the classic review, feedback aimed at the person made performance worse about a third of the time.
practices.safety: Their agenda, not a status report — and nothing here replaces a formal process when the subject is pay, conduct or someone’s job.

practices.title: Weekly delegation pass
practices.summary: Twenty minutes to take one recurring thing off your desk: kill it, automate it, or hand it over with an owner and a date.
practices.why: People reliably improve things by adding rather than removing — a robust experimental finding — so subtraction needs a booked slot or it never happens. That this particular weekly pass improves a company is practitioner experience.

practices.title: Quarterly think day
practices.summary: Once a quarter, two protected hours with no inputs: the three-year question, then what this quarter has to prove.
practices.why: Short structured written reflection has improved performance in field experiments, but stretching a fifteen-minute result to a quarterly half-day is extrapolation. A well-liked practice worth testing on yourself, not a settled finding.
practices.safety: Thinking time is not a substitute for talking to customers and the people doing the work.

practices.title: Cyclic sighing
practices.summary: Five minutes of double inhale through the nose, then a long, slow exhale.
practices.why: In a randomised trial that pitted five daily minutes of breathwork against five minutes of mindfulness meditation, cyclic sighing came out ahead on day-to-day mood and produced the larger drop in resting breathing rate. The long exhale is the working part; the second sip of air simply makes it possible.
practices.safety: A steadying tool, not treatment. Stop if you feel light-headed, and skip it entirely in water or behind the wheel. If you are pregnant or have a heart or breathing condition, check with your doctor before making it a daily habit.

practices.title: Goodwill practice
practices.summary: Five minutes directing plain, specific goodwill — someone easy, then yourself, then someone difficult.
practices.why: Warmth toward other people behaves like a trainable skill rather than a fixed trait, and short daily practice is associated with modest lifts in positive mood and in how connected people report feeling. The trials are small, short and hard to blind, so treat this as a fortnight’s experiment on yourself rather than a settled result.
practices.safety: Non-clinical, and not a way to force a feeling. If bringing a difficult person to mind opens more than you expected, stay with the easy one — or leave that step out.

practices.title: Body scan before sleep
practices.summary: Ten minutes lying down, moving attention slowly from the feet to the head.
practices.why: A body scan hands the mind a concrete, boring task at exactly the hour it most wants to plan and replay. Relaxation-based wind-downs are associated with modest improvements in how fast people fall asleep and how they rate the night — smaller than the effect of a consistent sleep and wake time, but it stacks on top of one.
practices.safety: Falling asleep partway through is fine — that is rather the point here. It is not a fix for insomnia; weeks of bad sleep is a conversation for a doctor or a sleep clinician.

practices.title: Open-monitoring sit
practices.summary: Five minutes noticing whatever shows up — sound, sensation, thought — naming it and letting it go.
practices.why: Rather than holding one anchor, you practise watching what the mind does. Meta-analyses of mindfulness training find real but modest effects on attention and stress, and open monitoring is the thinner half of that literature — it is rarely tested on its own. Plausible and useful; less certain than the ten-minute breath sit.
practices.safety: Non-clinical. Sitting with whatever arrives suits most people and unsettles some — if a sit leaves you distressed, detached from yourself, or reliably worse than you started, stop the practice and take it to a doctor or a therapist rather than pushing through. Meditation is not a substitute for professional care.

practices.title: Short technical block
practices.summary: Fifteen minutes on one part of your sport, most days, while you are still fresh.
practices.why: The same total practice time is worth more spread across many short sessions than piled into one long one — spacing is among the better-replicated findings in motor learning, and the gap between sessions is where the gain settles. Four honest fifteen-minute blocks beat one weekend hour.
practices.safety: Skill volume is still training volume — count it against your week, not on top of it. New movement patterns practised tired is where people get hurt, and pain is a stop sign, never a technique problem to push through.

practices.title: Shuffle the drills
practices.summary: Run the longer practice as mixed drills — a few reps of one thing, then switch, rather than a block of fifty.
practices.why: Blocked repetition — the bucket of a hundred identical shots — looks better inside the session and holds up worse a week later. Mixing the order feels clumsier at the time and tests better afterwards, an effect replicated across dozens of experiments. It is strongest in laboratory tasks and thinner in real sport, and a rank beginner may need some repetition first just to find the shape of the movement.
practices.safety: Switching drills often means switching movements cold — keep a real warm-up in front of it, and keep the hardest reps early while you are sharp.

practices.title: One cue, pointed outward
practices.summary: Write one cue before you practise, and aim it at the effect you want rather than at a body part.
practices.why: Instructions aimed outside the body — send it low over the net, push the floor away — reliably produce better movement than the same instruction aimed inward, at the wrist or the shoulder. The external-focus effect has been replicated across hundreds of small experiments, which makes it the most usable finding here and the one most amateur coaching quietly gets backwards.
practices.safety: A cue is an attention tool, not a safety brief. Anything a coach gave you for injury reasons stays regardless of how it is phrased.

practices.title: Film three reps
practices.summary: Once a week, film three reps on your phone and watch them back against this week’s one cue.
practices.why: What a movement feels like and what it looks like drift apart fast, and video is the cheapest way to close the gap. The evidence is moderate: video works when it arrives with a cue or a coach saying what to look at, and does little on its own — people new to a skill mostly cannot tell what they are seeing.
practices.safety: Check the rules where you train and keep other people, especially children, out of the frame. Video shows technique, never injury risk — soreness or a joint that keeps complaining is a physio question, not a camera angle.

practices.title: Practise the weak link
practices.summary: Twice a week, spend the block on the one thing you are worst at instead of the parts you enjoy.
practices.why: Practice aimed at a named weakness, with feedback on it, is what separates improving from accumulating mileage. The size of that claim is worth stating honestly: meta-analytic work found structured practice accounts for only a minority of the difference between athletes — on the order of a fifth of the variance in sport — with coaching, starting age, physiology and plain opportunity taking the rest. The ten-thousand-hours framing is folklore rather than a finding.
practices.safety: Your weakest movement is often the one your body is least prepared for — build the volume up over weeks, and take a weakness that hurts rather than merely frustrates to a coach or physio first.

practices.title: Rehearse it in your head
practices.summary: Ten minutes on a non-practice day running the movement in your head, at real speed, from inside your own body.
practices.why: Rehearsing a movement mentally beats doing nothing in meta-analyses spanning sport and surgical training, and it is one of the few things that keeps a skill warm on travel days. It is clearly weaker than real practice and fades if it starts replacing reps rather than topping them up.
practices.safety: If it is an injury keeping you off the pitch, rehearsal is not a return-to-play plan — that call belongs with a physio or doctor.

practices.title: The fortnightly weak-tie message
practices.summary: Every other week, one message to someone a step outside your close circle — a real question or a genuine offer, not a request for a favour.
practices.why: People hear about opportunities from contacts they rarely see rather than from close friends: a tight circle already knows what you know. That was a survey. The unusual part came later — randomised experiments on a large professional network changed which contacts tens of millions of people were shown, and moderately weak ties causally produced more job moves than either close ties or strangers. Extending that from an algorithm suggesting a contact to you writing on purpose is our own step.
practices.safety: A network is people, not a pipeline. Send the message you would be glad to receive, and expect nothing back from any single one — nothing here can promise a job, an introduction or a raise.

practices.title: The running accomplishments log
practices.summary: Ten Friday minutes writing down what you actually finished this week, in the plain words you would use outside your team.
practices.why: Review conversations run on what people can recall, and recall leans hard on the last few weeks. Appraisal research found a structured written record improves how faithfully work is remembered — though that work had managers recording other people, not people recording themselves, so we are borrowing it. The rest is practitioner folklore: kept all year, the review is written from evidence rather than from whatever the last fortnight left behind.
practices.safety: Your own work and your own part in shared work — a log that reads as a file on colleagues stops being honest, and stops being usable.

practices.title: Write the number before the conversation
practices.summary: Before a pay or terms conversation, write three things down: the figure you open with, what you would gladly accept, and the point where you walk away.
practices.why: Whoever names a figure first tends to drag the settlement toward it — anchoring is among the better-replicated findings in judgement research. Two honest limits: almost all of that work is lab and simulation rather than real pay talks, and the first-offer advantage shrinks or reverses when the other side knows the market far better than you, because a badly founded number mostly advertises how little you know. Writing the walk-away point down is what stops your own figure sliding under pressure.
practices.safety: Contracts, notice periods and pay law differ by country and employer — an employment lawyer or a union representative is the right next step before anything binding. Preparation changes what you ask for; it can never promise what you are offered.

practices.title: The quarterly mentor conversation
practices.summary: Once a quarter, forty-five minutes with someone a few steps ahead: one real problem, one question about how they read it, no status update.
practices.why: Meta-analyses find mentored people report better career satisfaction and modestly better objective outcomes — but the design cannot separate the mentoring from the selection, because mentors pick people who already look promising. Read that as weak and confounded. What survives is smaller and plainer: an outside view on your own work is cheap, and the people able to give it will never put it in your calendar for you.
practices.safety: A conversation about the work, not a channel for grievances — pay, conduct and anything about someone’s job belong in the formal process.

practices.title: Make the work visible
practices.summary: A short written weekly note to the people your work affects: what shipped, what is blocked, what is next.
practices.why: This is practitioner advice, and the genre is thick with survivorship stories. What is fair to say: decisions about your work get made in rooms you are not in, and what stands in for you there is whatever somebody half-remembers. A short written update makes that your own words instead. Experiments on self-promotion add a caution rather than a cheer — visible competence signals carry a social penalty, and a heavier one for women — so plain verifiable facts travel further than adjectives about yourself.
practices.safety: Name the people who did it with you, and claim only what you can evidence. If updates are treated as noise where you work, send narrower ones to fewer people rather than louder ones to more.

practices.title: Restart two dormant contacts
practices.summary: Once a quarter, pick two people you have genuinely lost touch with and restart the conversation with something specific.
practices.why: A field study asked executives to reconnect with contacts they had not spoken to in years: the dormant contacts were about as useful as their current ones and offered more that was new, having spent the intervening years somewhere else entirely. It was small, self-rated and uncontrolled, so read it as a reason to try rather than a measured effect. The plausible part is the mechanism — a dormant tie keeps the trust of an old one while having lost its redundancy.
practices.safety: Reconnect with people you would be pleased to hear from, and let a silence be an answer. Arriving after five years with an ask is how a dormant tie becomes a dead one.

practices.title: The same warm-up, every time
practices.summary: The same ten-minute warm-up before every session: easy cardio, then control, balance and speed.
practices.why: Structured warm-up programmes built around control, balance and progressive speed cut injury rates by roughly a third in cluster-randomised trials of team-sport players, which makes this one of the few genuinely well-tested ideas in injury prevention. Two honest caveats: the benefit tracked closely with how consistently squads actually did it, and the trials were in footballers rather than people warming up for a gym session.
practices.safety: A warm-up lowers risk, it does not remove it, and no warm-up makes a session your body is not ready for a safe one. Skip a movement that hurts rather than working around it — pain in a warm-up is information about the session you were about to do.

practices.title: Eccentric hamstring work
practices.summary: Two short sessions a week of slow, controlled eccentric hamstring work.
practices.why: Lengthening a muscle under load is the best-supported single exercise idea in prevention: randomised trials in footballers found roughly half as many new hamstring injuries in the groups doing this work. The catch is follow-through — surveys of professional squads found almost none kept it up, because the first fortnight makes you genuinely sore. Sprinting athletes are who was studied; for a general lifter this is a reasonable bet rather than a proven one.
practices.safety: Prevention work for a healthy hamstring, never rehabilitation for a hurt one — if you already have a hamstring problem, this is not the exercise for it and a physiotherapist is who should be choosing. Expect real soreness at first, add repetitions slowly, and stop for anything sharp rather than achy.

practices.title: The weekly load review
practices.summary: Ten Sunday minutes comparing last week’s training to the week you are about to plan.
practices.why: Sudden jumps in training are associated with injury across a lot of observational sports data, and the general advice — go up in steps you can repeat rather than leaps — is about as close to consensus as this field gets. What is not settled is any number attached to it. The popular acute-to-chronic workload ratio has been criticised hard on methodological grounds, and the one capped-increase rule actually put to a randomised trial in runners did not lower injury rates. So this is a review, not a formula: notice the jump and choose it on purpose, including in weeks when sleep, illness or stress mean you can absorb less.
practices.safety: A number on a page does not know how you feel; illness, thin sleep and a hard week all lower what you can take, and the plan should lose to any of them. Educational structure for your own training, not clinical judgement.

practices.title: The two-week niggle check
practices.summary: Five Sunday minutes naming any niggle — the same one two weeks running gets a professional.
practices.why: Most small training aches settle on their own within a couple of weeks, so the useful question is not what it is — IntentNorth cannot know that and will not guess — but how long it has been there and whether it is heading the right way. Weekly surveillance work in athletes turned up far more ongoing complaints than injury reports ever captured, because someone asked every week instead of waiting for people to stop. The two-week mark is a convention borrowed from ordinary clinical practice rather than a tested threshold, and it errs deliberately towards getting looked at sooner.
practices.safety: IntentNorth is not a clinician and this is not an assessment — nothing here names what is wrong with you or tells you how to fix it. Pain that persists past a couple of weeks, keeps worsening, wakes you at night, follows a fall or an impact, or arrives with numbness, giving way, or a joint that will not take weight is a doctor’s or physiotherapist’s job, not an app’s. Go sooner if you are worried, and go now rather than in two weeks for anything sudden and severe.

practices.title: The planned lighter week
practices.summary: Every fourth week, plan a deliberately lighter one — same sessions, less weight and volume.
practices.why: A lighter week every three to six is standard practice in nearly every serious programme, and the reasoning holds up: performance is maintained for weeks on substantially reduced training, so a planned easy week costs very little and buys back recovery you would otherwise take unplanned. Be clear about what is not known — no trial has shown that scheduled lighter weeks lower injury rates. This is coaching practice with a plausible mechanism, and its honest case is that the alternative is usually a break you did not get to choose.
practices.safety: A planned easy week is not a reason to push through in the weeks around it — if something hurts, waiting for the deload is the wrong answer. Persistent pain gets a professional’s opinion wherever you are in the block.

practices.title: Small session, most days
practices.summary: Twenty-five minutes on the creative work at the same time each weekday — before the day gets a vote on it.
practices.why: The one real experiment here compared academics who wrote in short scheduled sessions against those who waited for a good long stretch: the scheduled writers produced several times the pages, and more new ideas, over the same weeks. It is a small, decades-old study whose daily arm also carried an accountability contingency, so read that gap as an argument for the shape rather than a number to expect. What the shape reliably buys is smaller and certain — a session that already has a time does not have to be decided on.
practices.safety: Twenty-five minutes you keep beats ninety you cancel — shrink the session before you drop the day. If the weekend binge is genuinely working for you, this protocol has nothing to offer.

practices.title: The incubation walk
practices.summary: Twenty minutes walking away from a draft you are stuck on — no phone, no podcast, the problem left deliberately open.
practices.why: Stepping away from an unsolved problem beats grinding on: pooled across roughly a hundred experiments, a break improved later solutions, most of all on open-ended problems and when the break was filled with something undemanding — which a walk is. Separately, walking raised how many ideas people generated compared with sitting. Both effects are modest and measured on short laboratory tasks; nobody has shown they carry all the way to finishing a novel.
practices.safety: This only does anything after real effort on the problem. A walk taken before you are properly stuck is just a walk — a good thing, but not this one.

practices.title: The volume pass
practices.summary: One weekly half-hour making as many rough attempts as you can — one fixed small format, nothing judged until the timer stops.
practices.why: Across whole careers, the people with the most admired works also made the most works overall, and their hit rate stayed roughly constant — so more attempts is largely how the good ones appear. That pattern is archival and correlational, and a weekly volume session has never been tested as such. The often-repeated ceramics-class story, where the group graded on quantity supposedly out-produced the group graded on quality, is a parable with no study behind it and we do not count it as evidence.
practices.safety: Rough means rough, and the small format is the point — evidence that tight constraints help creative work is genuinely mixed. If the pass turns into polishing one piece it has become an ordinary session, which is fine, but it is no longer this.

practices.title: Ship it monthly
practices.summary: Once a month, a named date when something actually goes out — published, sent, played, hung, or handed to one real person.
practices.why: Work with no delivery date drifts, and the firmest evidence here is about the drift rather than the work: students who set their own spaced deadlines finished better than those working toward one distant one. None of that measured whether what got made was any good, and other experiments have found that working under evaluation and time pressure can flatten creativity rather than sharpen it. Hence monthly rather than weekly, and an audience of one being enough.
practices.safety: A date, not a verdict on you. If shipping has come to mean performing for an audience you dread, make the audience smaller before you make the deadline harder.

practices.title: Empty the notebook
practices.summary: Five minutes at the end of the day moving every idea you caught into the one place you will actually look again.
practices.why: This is craft folklore, and we grade it that way: no trial has shown that keeping an idea book makes anybody more creative. What is better supported is narrower and indirect — handing something you mean to remember to an external store you trust measurably frees attention for the next thing. That argues for the sweep, not for the payoff. It costs five minutes, so run it for a month and keep it only if the notebook is fuller and your head is quieter.
practices.safety: One place, not five. A capture system that needs maintaining has quietly become the creative project.

practices.title: Anchored wake time
practices.summary: One wake time, seven days a week — feet on the floor within half an hour of it, weekends included.
practices.why: Wake time is the lever with the most leverage in sleep, and the one people give away first. Holding it steady holds the whole clock steady: light hits the eyes at the same hour, sleep pressure builds on the same schedule, and bedtime starts arriving on its own instead of being negotiated. You cannot decide to fall asleep, but you can decide to get up. A large accelerometer cohort found that how regular people’s sleep was predicted mortality more strongly than how long they slept — observational, and it cannot prove direction, but it points at the same behaviour.
practices.safety: Hold the wake time and let bedtime follow it — do not hold both ends by shortening sleep. If weeks of a steady wake time still leave you exhausted, that is worth taking to a doctor rather than tightening the rule.

practices.title: Lights down
practices.summary: Two hours before bed, drop the household lights to lamps and put the bright screens down.
practices.why: The evening eye is far more light-sensitive than it feels: ordinary room light in the hours before bed measurably delays the body’s night-time signalling, and controlled trials of bright screens have pushed the body clock later. What is less settled is the household version — trials that simply ask adults to dim the lamps and put the phone away show small and inconsistent effects on sleep itself. A cheap, physiologically sensible bet rather than a proven result.
practices.safety: A lighting habit, not a fix for a sleep disorder. If you are lying awake most nights regardless, a doctor or sleep clinician is the better next step.

practices.title: Warm shower, cool room
practices.summary: A warm shower or bath about ninety minutes before bed, into a bedroom kept deliberately cool.
practices.why: Sleep starts with a drop in core body temperature, and you can help that along. Warming the skin sends blood to the surface, and when you step out the body sheds heat faster than it otherwise would — the warm shower works by cooling you, which is why timing matters more than temperature. A review of small randomised trials found people fell asleep roughly ten minutes faster when the bath came an hour or two before lights out. The cool-room half rests on thinner, mostly laboratory evidence.
practices.safety: Warm, not scalding, and stand up slowly — hot water can leave you light-headed. Check with a doctor first if you are pregnant or have a heart or circulation condition.

practices.title: Alcohol cutoff
practices.summary: Last drink at least four hours before bed — nothing about whether you drink, only about when you stop.
practices.why: Alcohol is the most convincing sleep impostor there is: it gets you under faster, so it feels like it helped. Laboratory work is consistent about what happens next — REM sleep is suppressed, the first half of the night is unusually deep, and as the alcohol clears the second half fragments into more awakenings. You wake with the hours logged and none of the repair. The body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, so the fix is timing rather than abstinence.
practices.safety: A timing habit for ordinary drinking, and nothing more. If cutting down or stopping feels difficult, or you drink daily, that is a conversation for a doctor — not something to manage with a scheduling app.

practices.title: Short nap, early
practices.summary: Twenty minutes or ninety, never in between — and nothing after mid-afternoon.
practices.why: Short naps of ten to twenty minutes reliably lift alertness in controlled studies and leave you clear-headed, because you surface before the deepest sleep arrives. Wake out of that deep stage — roughly where a forty-five minute nap lands you — and you get the groggy half-hour that gives napping its bad name. The timing half is reasoning rather than trial evidence: a nap spends sleep pressure you were saving for tonight, so the later it runs, the more it borrows from the night.
practices.safety: Skip naps entirely while you are struggling to fall asleep at night — they work against the pressure you need. Regular daytime sleepiness despite full nights is worth raising with a doctor.

practices.title: The twenty-minute rule
practices.summary: Still awake after about twenty minutes? Get up, sit somewhere dim and dull, and go back only when sleepy.
practices.why: Lying in bed frustrated teaches the bed something. The longer you spend awake there, the more reliably the room starts to signal alertness rather than sleep, and the association builds night after night without your help. Getting up breaks the pairing. Do not clock-watch — twenty minutes is a feel, not a measurement. Of all the components inside cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, this is the one with the most standalone randomised evidence behind it.
practices.safety: This is one piece of a structured programme, not the programme. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the front-line approach clinicians recommend for persistent sleeplessness, and IntentNorth does not deliver it — if bad nights have run for weeks, see a doctor or a sleep clinician.

practices.title: End-range strength block
practices.summary: Twice a week, finish lifting with slow, loaded work at the very end of your range.
practices.why: In head-to-head comparisons, strength work taken through a full range improves flexibility about as much as stretching does — and the range you own under load is the range that holds up when you are tired or off balance. Long, heavy holds at length are also how tendons appear to adapt, though that work is small and short-term.
practices.safety: Light loads first: add range before you add weight. End-range positions are where a joint is least protected — hold them, never bounce into them. Sharp or lingering joint pain is a reason to stop and see a clinician, not to push through.

practices.title: Targeted long-hold stretching
practices.summary: Four evenings a week, hold two or three stretches for the one range you actually want back.
practices.why: Static stretching reliably improves range of motion when the same positions are held for a few minutes across a week — part real tissue change, part learning to tolerate the position, and both count. It fades if you stop. The old warning that stretching ruins your lifting is overstated: short holds barely move strength, and the measurable drop-off shows up mainly after long holds tested immediately afterwards, which is why this sits in the evening.
practices.safety: Slow and held, never bounced. A strong stretch feeling is fine; sharp or radiating pain is not. Stretching has not been shown to lower overall injury risk, so it is no substitute for warming up properly and loading sensibly.

practices.title: Ankle and hip prep before leg day
practices.summary: Ten minutes of active ankle and hip range before the days you squat, hinge or lunge.
practices.why: Ankle and hip range are the two limiters that decide what a squat can look like — when the ankle runs out of range, depth drops and the knee tends to drift inward. Controlled biomechanics work shows that link clearly. What is far less certain is whether restoring range prevents anything, so read this as making today’s session better, not as insurance.
practices.safety: Warm, active range — not long relaxed holds immediately before heavy lifting. If a range only appears when something forces you into it, work with what you can reach under your own power instead.

practices.title: Thoracic and shoulder reset
practices.summary: An eight-minute afternoon block of upper-back extension, rotation and overhead range.
practices.why: Getting the arms overhead asks the mid-back to extend and rotate; when it will not, the shoulder makes up the difference. Small controlled trials show thoracic mobility work improves mid-back and shoulder range in the short term. The larger claim — that it corrects posture or prevents shoulder pain — is not well supported, and posture on its own is a weak predictor of who hurts.
practices.safety: Stay inside ranges you can reach under your own power. Numbness, tingling or pain running down an arm is a clinician question, not a signal to mobilise harder.

practices.title: Movement snacks
practices.summary: Once an hour on working days, stand up and move through two or three full-range shapes.
practices.why: The firm evidence here is metabolic: breaking up long sitting with brief movement lowers post-meal glucose and insulin in controlled crossover trials. The joint argument — that frequent variety keeps you moving better than one dedicated session does — is plausible and largely untested, so this earns its place on the metabolic side, with the range work as a bonus.
practices.safety: Genuinely brief and easy — if a break leaves you needing to recover, it was a workout. Nothing here is loaded or forced.

practices.title: Balance and single-leg practice
practices.summary: Three short sessions a week: standing on one leg, plus slow single-leg strength.
practices.why: Balance and functional training is among the best-supported interventions in exercise science for reducing falls — but that evidence sits in adults over 65 and does not automatically transfer to someone in their forties. What holds at our age is narrower: balance is trainable, it fades quietly from midlife onward, and single-leg work exposes side-to-side differences a barbell lets you hide.
practices.safety: Practise beside a wall or worktop you can grab. Progress by closing your eyes or narrowing your stance before adding load. Dizziness or unexplained loss of balance belongs with a doctor, not with more practice.

practices.title: The weekly long one
practices.summary: One longer easy session a week — run, ride, swim or row — at a pace you could talk through.
practices.why: Every serious endurance plan is built around one long easy session, and total weekly volume is the training variable that tracks most closely with how an event day goes. That link is largely observational, and the long session has almost never been isolated and tested on its own, so the shape is well-worn practice rather than a proven ingredient. Its real work is teaching legs and head what the hour past comfortable feels like, before the event is the first place you meet it.
practices.safety: Conversational the whole way — if the last third is a grind every single week, the session is too long rather than you too soft. Grow it in minutes, not chapters, and skip it outright when you are ill or badly slept.

practices.title: Mark the hard days
practices.summary: Ten Sunday minutes naming next week’s one or two hard sessions; everything else runs easy.
practices.why: Endurance athletes who train well spend roughly four fifths of their sessions at an easy, conversational effort and keep the hard work to a small deliberate slice. Controlled comparisons exist, but nearly all are in already-trained athletes; in recreational runners the trials are smaller and results go both ways. What is not in doubt is the failure it fixes — easy days run slightly too hard and hard days not hard enough, so every session lands in the same grey middle.
practices.safety: Two hard sessions a week is a ceiling for most people, not a target. If a hard day is still in your legs three days later, it belongs in the easy column until it is not.

practices.title: Lifting for the run
practices.summary: Twice a week, 30 minutes of heavy lower-body lifting and a few short hops, away from the long session.
practices.why: The most underused finding in endurance training: controlled trials, and the reviews pooling them, find that heavy or explosive strength work improves running economy — the oxygen cost of holding a given pace — and the times that follow, without the weight gain runners fear. The trials are mostly small and short and run in people already training. Heavy and few repetitions is what was tested; circuits to exhaustion are a different thing wearing the same name.
practices.safety: Load you control through a full range, and keep hops low and few while tendons learn them. Leave a day between this and the long session. New to lifting, or carrying a niggle — have a coach or physio watch the first sessions.

practices.title: Taper into the event
practices.summary: For the final two weeks: cut total volume by roughly half, keep the sharp bits, keep the frequency.
practices.why: Pooled trials in trained endurance athletes credit a well-run taper with a small but real gain — a couple of per cent, which across a long event is minutes. The version that came out best was a progressive volume cut of roughly 40 to 60% over about two weeks, intensity kept, session frequency largely unchanged; resting completely does worse than tapering. Nearly all of that work is in trained athletes, so a first-timer can trust the direction and discount the size.
practices.safety: Feeling flat and restless mid-taper is ordinary, and not a reason to put a session back. Nothing new in the last fortnight — not the shoes, not the session type. Pain that changes your stride is a clinician question before the event rather than after it.

practices.title: Shorter, quicker steps
practices.summary: On two easy runs a week, ten minutes holding steps about 5–10% quicker and lighter than they fall on their own.
practices.why: Take slightly quicker, shorter steps at the same speed and the load going through the knee and hip on each step measurably drops — gait-lab studies show that repeatedly. What they do not show is that changing it prevents injuries or makes anyone faster; those outcome trials are few, small and short. A cheap adjustment with a measured mechanism and an unproven payoff.
practices.safety: A nudge, not an overhaul — a few per cent, on easy runs only, and never in the weeks right before an event. Changing how you run moves load around rather than removing it, so a new ache in a new place means stop.

practices.title: Spaced review
practices.summary: Fifteen minutes a day back over older material — the oldest and the shakiest first.
practices.why: Meeting the same material again after a gap, instead of in one long sitting, is among the most replicated findings in learning research: hundreds of controlled comparisons across ages, subjects and delays, and the advantage grows the longer you need to hold on to it. Same total minutes, far more of it still there in a month.
practices.safety: Educational structure for ordinary study, nothing more. Memory or attention trouble that genuinely worries you is a conversation for a doctor, not a study habit.

practices.title: The blank page
practices.summary: End each study session by closing everything and writing what you remember — then check it.
practices.why: Pulling material out of your head beats putting it in again, and it is the best-supported study behaviour there is: meta-analyses covering hundreds of experiments find medium-to-large gains on later tests, in real classrooms as well as labs, and the gap widens the longer you wait. Checking afterwards is part of the practice — recall without feedback keeps your mistakes.
practices.safety: It feels harder and less productive than rereading — that is the mechanism working, not a sign it is going badly. If a session ends in defeat rather than effort, make it shorter.

practices.title: Interleaved practice
practices.summary: One weekly session mixing the different problem or piece types instead of drilling one.
practices.why: Drilling one type until it clicks feels like progress; shuffling types feels worse and tests better a week later, because mixing makes you work out which approach a problem needs rather than just running the one you were handed. Several controlled experiments and a randomised classroom trial in maths point the same way — the benefit is clearest where the types are easy to confuse.
practices.safety: Mix what you have already met, not what you have never seen. A genuine first pass at something new is still best taken one thing at a time.

practices.title: Explain it to yourself
practices.summary: Twice a week, stop at each section and say why it is true and how it fits what you know.
practices.why: Asking why something would be so, and tying a new fact to something you already hold, turns reading into thinking, and in controlled studies it beats another pass over the same page. The effect is consistent but has been tested mostly on short material in short sessions, so how far it carries into a long, hard subject is the open part.

practices.title: Teach it back
practices.summary: Once a week, explain the week’s material to someone — out loud, from memory, no notes.
practices.why: Explaining without notes is recall with an audience, and the sentence you cannot finish is the gap you did not know you had. Studies on expecting to teach, and on explaining aloud, mostly find modest gains, but they are smaller and patchier than the retrieval work underneath them — and a weekly session is our packaging of the idea, not a tested protocol.
practices.safety: An empty room, a voice memo or a willing friend all count. Nobody has to be conscripted into being your audience.

practices.title: Questions, not highlights
practices.summary: Ten minutes ending each reading session: turn the pages into three questions, no highlighter.
practices.why: In the best-known review of study techniques, highlighting and rereading came out near the bottom — they make material feel familiar without doing much for what you can recall later. The same ten minutes spent writing questions you will have to answer next week puts the effort where the evidence is. Writing your own questions is less studied than answering ready-made ones, so this is the softer half of a well-tested idea.

practices.title: Phone parked before the block
practices.summary: Phone in another room — not face-down, not in a pocket — before the day’s focus block starts.
practices.why: The well-known experiments claiming a phone on the desk quietly eats working memory are small, and at least one careful attempt to repeat the headline result found nothing, so the “brain drain” story is not settled and we do not lean on it. The harder-to-argue part is simpler: a phone within reach gets picked up, and every pickup is a switch you then pay for twice. Another room removes the decision instead of asking you to win it.
practices.safety: A working arrangement, nothing more — never a fix for an attention disorder. If focus has been a lifelong difficulty across school, work and home alike, that belongs with a doctor or psychologist rather than a phone drawer.

practices.title: Notification audit
practices.summary: Roughly monthly: switch off every alert that is not a person, then check the rest in two or three set windows.
practices.why: Randomised field experiments have had people batch their email or silence notifications for a week at a time, and the batched weeks came back with less distraction and lower reported stress than the always-on ones. Samples are modest and outcomes self-reported, and nobody has shown this makes you produce more — the honest claim is a calmer day, not a more productive one.

practices.title: Close the loop before you switch
practices.summary: One task at a time, and sixty seconds before each switch: where you stopped, and the next concrete move.
practices.why: Part of your attention stays behind with the last task when you move to the next one, and it lingers longest when that task was abandoned mid-thought. The studies are small and largely laboratory work, but the mechanism is plausible and a follow-up found that writing a short note about where to pick it up reduced the carry-over. Treat the famous twenty-odd-minutes-to-refocus figure as folklore: it comes from one small observational study and was never a constant.
practices.safety: Ordinary difficulty switching tasks is normal, and this is a work habit for it. Attention trouble that has followed you through every setting for years is a clinician’s question, not a scheduling one.

practices.title: Outdoors, nothing in your ears
practices.summary: Fifteen minutes outside in the middle of the day — no podcast, no calls, no phone in your hand.
practices.why: Green, undemanding surroundings appear to let effortful attention recover in a way that swapping one screen for another does not, and there are real experiments behind that rather than survey data alone. But effect sizes swing wildly between studies, several of the most-quoted ones are tiny, and the broader green-space literature is observational. What we are confident about is the removal of input; how much you get back is genuinely uncertain.

practices.title: A real break every hour
practices.summary: Three to five minutes properly away from the screen each hour — stand, look far away, move.
practices.why: This one has been meta-analysed and the answer is smaller than the internet suggests: short breaks reliably lift how tired and how energetic people feel, and have close to no measurable effect on how much or how well they work. Worth having anyway, because fatigue is what ends good afternoons — but it is a comfort finding, not a performance one.

practices.title: The off switch
practices.summary: A protected weekday evening window where work is not checked, not answered and not chewed over.
practices.why: Recovery research draws a line between being off work and feeling off work. The thing that keeps predicting how you arrive the next morning is psychological detachment — whether the mind actually left. Diary and longitudinal studies across many occupations find that people who detach in the evening report less fatigue and better mood the following day. The effect is consistent and modest rather than dramatic, and there is an honest catch: detachment is hardest exactly when the load is highest, which is when it would help most.
practices.safety: Structure for an ordinary heavy week, nothing more. If the mind will not leave work whatever you do, or the tiredness does not lift on a holiday, that is a workload conversation — and often a doctor or therapist conversation — rather than a scheduling problem.

practices.title: Closing the working day
practices.summary: Ten minutes at the end of the working day: loose ends written down, tomorrow’s first move named, one deliberate line that says you are done.
practices.why: Unfinished work keeps interrupting attention until it has a plan, and a small experimental literature suggests writing the plan is enough to quieten it even though nothing got finished. Add the boundary-crossing idea — that moving between roles goes better with a marker — and you have a cheap, plausible ritual that hands the detachment window a clean start. Plausible is the honest word: the underlying studies are small, and the ritual as a package has been described far more often than tested.
practices.safety: A closing marker, not a productivity system. If the list is genuinely undoable inside contracted hours, ten minutes of tidying will not change that — the size of the list is what to raise with whoever sets it.

practices.title: Read the nerves as readiness
practices.summary: Before something that matters, name the arousal and relabel it as the body getting ready rather than as a warning.
practices.why: In laboratory experiments, people told that a fast heart and quick breathing are the body mobilising went on to perform better under pressure and showed a cardiovascular pattern closer to challenge than to threat. The instruction is a few sentences long and the difference shows up in the same session, which makes it unusually easy to try on yourself. The limits are the ordinary ones: mostly students, mostly single sessions, and very little on what a year of it does.
practices.safety: This is for ordinary performance nerves — a presentation, an interview, a hard conversation. It is not a method for panic attacks or for fear that is steering your choices; those belong with a doctor or a therapist. Relabelling a feeling also does nothing to change a situation that genuinely needs changing.

practices.title: Move it out on the heavy days
practices.summary: On the two heaviest days of the week, twenty to thirty minutes of easy movement placed inside the day rather than saved for later.
practices.why: The dependable half of this is direct: across many randomised trials, regular aerobic activity lowers how stressed and how flat people report feeling, at intensities well below anything athletic. The shakier half is the buffering claim — that being fitter blunts the body’s reaction to a stressor — where findings are mixed and effects shrink in better-controlled studies. Book it for the mood and the head-clearing, which holds up.
practices.safety: Easy-to-moderate means you could hold a conversation. This sits beside training rather than on top of it — in a heavy week movement should subtract load, never add it. New chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness on exertion means stopping and seeing a doctor.

practices.title: Read your own baseline
practices.summary: Once a week, read resting heart rate and heart-rate variability as a multi-week trend against your own baseline — never as a daily verdict.
practices.why: Heart-rate variability really does track autonomic state, and a sustained fall alongside a rising resting heart rate is a fair hint that load, short sleep, alcohol or a coming illness is stacking up. What the numbers will not carry is the weight most products put on them. Healthy people differ several-fold in absolute values, single readings swing on posture, breathing rate and whichever algorithm your device uses, and the work showing guided decisions beat a fixed plan comes mostly from small endurance-athlete trials. Weekly direction against your own baseline is roughly as much signal as this carries.
practices.safety: A number can quietly become one more thing to fail at. If checking leaves you more anxious than informed, stop checking — nothing is lost. These readings say nothing reliable about illness on their own: symptoms go to a doctor, and anything that feels like a heart rhythm problem goes there promptly.

practices.title: The six-area check
practices.summary: Roughly monthly, twenty minutes naming which of six things is actually wrong — workload, control, reward, community, fairness or values — and who you will say it to out loud.
practices.why: Burnout research has been fairly steady for three decades about where the problem sits: a sustained mismatch between a person and their job, most often too much work with too little say over how it is done. That conclusion is awkward for wellbeing apps and worth stating plainly — reviews of workplace trials find that changing the work outperforms training the individual, and the individual programmes that do help tend to produce small effects that fade. Naming the specific mismatch turns a vague sense of being fried into something a manager, a peer or a professional can act on.
practices.safety: A structural review, not a resilience exercise, and the limit deserves saying plainly: no breathing practice and no evening routine will fix a job with an impossible workload or no control over how the work is done. If the honest answer is that the work itself has to change, the next steps are your manager, your union or professional body, or a different job. And if you are at dread, numbness, or thoughts of not wanting to be here, that is a doctor or therapist today — not a monthly review.

practices.title: The message you nearly didn’t send
practices.summary: Five minutes to message someone you have drifted from — no ask, no plan, just that you thought of them.
practices.why: People are poor judges of this one. Across repeated experiments, senders consistently underestimated how much a small out-of-the-blue check-in mattered to the person on the other end, and the gap was widest exactly where contact had lapsed and the message came as a surprise. "They probably don’t want to hear from me" is the belief the evidence argues with, which is why this aims at the belief rather than at your calendar.
practices.safety: Send it and let it go — a slow reply, or none, is usually a busy week rather than a verdict. Where someone has asked for space, respect that instead.

practices.title: Answer the good news properly
practices.summary: Ten minutes to go back to the good news a friend shared and reply like you mean it: ask for the detail, say why it lands.
practices.why: How you answer someone’s good news appears to matter as much as how you answer their bad news. Diary and lab work links warm, curious replies with both people feeling closer afterwards, while a flat acknowledgement reads as indifference even when none was meant. Most of this research was done inside couples and measures how people already respond more often than it changes it, so the direction is reasonably solid and the size is not.

practices.title: The standing thing
practices.summary: One activity with the same people at the same hour every week, decided once so nobody has to organise it again.
practices.why: Adult friendships mostly form as a by-product of repeated shared time rather than from deciding to be closer, and familiarity does much of the early work. A standing slot removes the weekly negotiation that quietly kills most plans. The count-the-hours research everyone quotes here is a single study on a modest sample using recalled estimates, so we keep the direction — ordinary hours side by side accumulate into closeness — and leave its specific thresholds alone.

practices.title: Belong to something that meets
practices.summary: Turn up to one group that meets whether or not you do — a club, a team, a choir, a regular table.
practices.why: A sizeable body of research on group membership and health finds that the number of groups people genuinely feel part of tracks with steadier mood and better wellbeing through hard stretches, and that losing memberships — a move, a job change, retirement — is often when people come unstuck. Most of it is cohort and longitudinal work, so read belonging as protective company you take part in rather than something the group does to you.
practices.safety: Attendance is the whole practice — a group you dread is the wrong group, not a discipline problem. Swap it rather than defend it.

practices.title: Who you actually miss
practices.summary: Roughly monthly, fifteen written minutes: who you feel close to, who you have drifted from, and one name to move on this month.
practices.why: Being short of company and feeling unknown are different problems with different answers, and a full calendar hides the second one well. Large observational studies link both the countable version and the felt version to worse long-term health — a strong and consistent association, but drawn from watching populations rather than from showing that adding contacts changes the outcome. The written pass itself is our structure: a way to catch the drift while it is still cheap to reverse.
practices.safety: A prompt for noticing, not a scorecard on your friendships. Loneliness that sits heavily for months, or arrives alongside low mood, is worth raising with a doctor rather than writing your way through.

practices.title: Annual capacity benchmark
practices.summary: Once a year, the same three tests on the same morning: a timed hard walk or run, a hang or loaded carry for time, and a one-leg balance hold.
practices.why: Aerobic capacity and grip strength are two of the sharpest predictors of how long people live in very large observational studies — hundreds of thousands of adults followed for years, with the gap between fittest and least fit wider than for most risk factors anyone talks about. Both capacities respond to training, but no one has shown that moving your number moves your lifespan, so read this as a signal about your trajectory rather than a lever you pull.
practices.safety: A hard-effort test is genuinely hard: build to it over weeks, and stop for chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness. Talk to your doctor before testing if you have a heart condition, are pregnant, or have been away from training. A field test only estimates — a real laboratory measurement is something a doctor or exercise physiologist orders and interprets.

practices.title: Floor-to-stand practice
practices.summary: Twice a week: lower yourself to the floor and stand back up five times with as little hand support as you can manage.
practices.why: In a cohort of roughly two thousand adults aged 51 to 80, those who needed more support to get down to the floor and back up were more likely to die in the years that followed. That is one population, scored by eye, and anyone who can do it unaided is probably healthier in a dozen unmeasured ways — so treat the link as a hint rather than a finding to lean on. The practice earns its place regardless: getting off the floor unaided is a large part of what decides whether later decades are lived independently.
practices.safety: Practise next to a wall or a sturdy chair, on a soft surface, hands available — the aim is to need them less over months, not to risk a fall today. Knee, hip or back trouble, or any history of falls, is a conversation with a doctor or physiotherapist before you start.

practices.title: Blood pressure check
practices.summary: One morning a week, before coffee: sit still for five minutes, take two readings a minute apart, and write both down in the same place.
